item.content:encoded:
CINCINNATI — The Los Angeles Dodgers have kept open the possibility that Shohei Ohtani will return before the end of the regular season, though they are up against a running clock.
Any progress is good progress for the Dodgers’ most important piece, so it was a good thing when Ohtani started up activity Tuesday and Thursday and didn’t report any discomfort in his bothersome biceps, balky left knee and tight neck.
“Feels normal…ish,” manager Dave Roberts said Thursday morning.
Advertisement
Ohtani went on the injured list late last week, ending a months-long injury saga and giving him a maximum of five additional regular season games to play in before another the playoffs. He is eligible to return as soon as Sept. 23, though Roberts did not commit to that timeline.
There are still steps for Ohtani to take. He swung off a tee on Tuesday, had Wednesday off from baseball activity and could hit off a coach’s pitching by the end of the week. He will need to face some sort of live pitching before he appears in a game and even then, the maximum of five games does not feel like a lot for him to get his timing right.
Especially since, given how the Dodgers tried kicking the can on shelving Ohtani, he will return after having taken just four plate appearances since Sept. 2. Ohtani, clearly compromised by his nagging injuries, had just six hits over his final 49 at-bats before hitting the IL.
They still need Ohtani, even if he is not 100 percent. The oldest lineup in baseball has shown its age. Even if Ohtani’s role on the postseason roster is simply to provide the threat of launching a ball into the seats, that is valuable in their quest for a third consecutive World Series title. The Dodgers’ first road trip without Ohtani since his arrival in 2024 has been noticeably different.
“It’s been a weird feeling because I talk to him all the time in the clubhouse,” Yoshinobu Yamamoto joked through interpreter Yoshihiro Sonoda. Yamamoto has instead had to rely on Roki Sasaki, “but he doesn’t really talk to me.”
Díaz’ place in the bullpen
Edwin Díaz will return to the Dodgers on Friday, but not as the club’s closer. Nothing is guaranteed for the guy the Dodgers gave $69 million to solve their ninth-inning problem and who now could be on the bubble for the postseason roster thanks to his 11.85 ERA.
Díaz, who has made only 16 major-league appearances thanks to arthroscopic elbow surgery and a later neck issue, has also pitched poorly in rehab. A five-run blowup on Sunday with Triple-A Oklahoma City caused the Dodgers to delay Díaz’s return. But a scoreless inning on Wednesday — albeit one in which Díaz gave up a 104 mph double and did not induce a single swing-and-miss — was enough for the Dodgers to bring him back to the big leagues.
“It was his best one yet,” Roberts said of Díaz, whose has a low bar to clear.
Advertisement
Díaz will return in lower-leverage situations and have to show prove over the final week of the regular season he deserves a spot in the Dodgers’ postseason bullpen, even if their list of right-handed relief options is thinning.
“I think like anything it should be a meritocracy,” Roberts said. “You have to earn the right of opportunities but then you also got to perform, right?”
Edgardo Henriquez was the club’s most trusted reliever before he went on the injured list on Monday. Subsequent imaging showed what Roberts dubbed a “low-grade” back strain, and the manager said he was “hopeful” that Henriquez could still be a postseason option.
Another potential solution, Sasaki, is now needed in the rotation after Blake Snell exited Wednesday’s start with left groin tightness. The Dodgers will know more about Snell’s fate once they return to Los Angeles and potentially get imaging done, but Sasaki is currently slated to pitch at some point next week against the San Diego Padres.
The Dodgers have also been cagey about Tyler Glasnow’s status. Roberts was vague after Glasnow’s last start, but said the right-hander “didn’t feel great” going into it. The Dodgers sent Glasnow directly to Los Angeles afterwards rather than have him travel with the club to Cincinnati, and Roberts said Glasnow’s preparation for Friday’s start has otherwise been normal.
Pages’ return imminent
Andy Pages will “very likely” return to the Dodgers’ lineup without playing in rehab games at some point during the six-game home stand that opens Friday. Pages has progressed quickly from left hand fracture and the Dodgers are banking on the All-Star’s defensive value in center field despite the chances he’ll struggle on offensive.
Pages moved from hitting softer baseballs to hitting normal ones this week and will hit off the Trajekt Arc machine to simulate live at-bats. There aren’t a lot of games to go around on a rehab assignment, anyway, though Oklahoma City did clinch a postseason berth on Wednesday (those games start next week).

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are expected to activate Edwin Díaz from the injured list on Friday, but he will not slot back into closing games right away.
According to the Orange County Register's Bill Plunkett, Dave Roberts said the plan is to activate Díaz for the San Francisco Giants series, but to have him pitch in "low leverage" situations for the time being. Roberts also called the bullpen a "meritocracy" and said that Díaz needs to prove himself.
Díaz was the National League Reliever of the Year last year and has won three career Reliever of the Year Awards. The Dodgers gave him a three-year, $69 million deal in the offseason, but he has had a terrible season.
Through his first six games, he had a 10.50 ERA and blew a save. He then underwent a procedure to remove loose bodies from his elbow. After returning, he posted a 12.91 ERA in nine games, blowing three saves. The Dodgers placed him on the injured list with neck inflammation on Aug. 18 and are hoping for the best version of him this time.
Díaz has noted that he thinks fixing his arm angle will help him, but it's a results-based business. He will have to prove he can pitch like the Dodgers expected him to be, and the Dodgers need him more now than ever.
Since the All-Star Break, the Dodgers bullpen has a 4.34 ERA, ranked 20th in baseball. The bullpen also has a 10.4% walk rate, the seventh-worst in baseball. Dodgers relievers have also given up 24 home runs in the second half. If Díaz can come back and pitch like an All-Star, it will go a long way in fixing the bullpen woes. The team is currently without Edgardo Henriquez, so they need a reliable right-hander in the bullpen.
Roberts also confirmed that outfielder Andy Pages (hand) is expected to rejoin LA during upcoming homestand without requiring a minor-league rehab assignment.

Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said it's "very likely" that outfielder Andy Pages (hand) will be activated during the team's upcoming homestand, per Jack Harris of the California Post. Los Angeles begins a six-game homestand on Friday. Pages has been sidelined since August 21 by a fractured left hand, but it appears he is now on the doorstep of a return to the big leagues. Across 550 plate appearances before the injury, the 25-year-old hit .272/.338/.458 with 21 home runs, 80 RBI, 72 runs scored, and 12 stolen bases. Pages was the Dodgers' everyday center fielder before getting hurt and should resume that role upon his return. Once activated, Pages profiles as a must-start outfielder for fantasy managers.--Will Brady
Source: California Post - Jack Harris

The lefty-swinger is hitting .192 across just 63 plate appearances against left-handed pitching, so his big-side platoon role limits his fantasy value to some degree. However, Peters owns an .824 OPS against right-handers and brings a balanced profile at the plate that allows him to provide modest production across all five fantasy categories. After hitting six home runs across 87 plate appearances in August, the 26-year-old has gone without a homer in his first 56 trips to the plate in September. Still, Peters hits for average and should continue to provide steady run production in stretches where the White Sox face a string of right-handed starting pitchers. item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers lost to the Cincinnati Reds, 6-2, on Wednesday and fell to 92-60 on the year.
Blake Snell pitched just one inning before he was removed from his start due to groin tightness. After Blake Treinen pitched a clean second inning, the Reds took advantage of the impromptu bullpen game and halted any potential NL West-clinching celebrations.
Offensively, Mookie Betts still shined with a three-hit outing and Will Smith also enjoyed a multi-hit night. The backstop appears to be gaining his footing once again, hitting .273 with three RBIs in his last seven games.
Ahead of the eventual defeat, the Dodgers surprisingly designated an outfielder for assignment hitting .218 in his first 20 MLB games in order to make room on the roster to activate All-Star right-hander Kris Bubic. Though it wasn't the most ideal situation to be making his debut with the two-time defending champions, Bubic struck out two in a scoreless eighth inning.
After the game, both Snell and manager Dave Roberts provided an update on the left-hander's injury. Snell revealed that he felt his groin "grab" during a pregame bullpen and knew then he shouldn't go beyond the first inning. Regardless, he said he "should be good" to make another start before the postseason.
Roberts, however, wasn't as sure.
“It’s a possibility,” Roberts said. “I like where his head is at, but he just can’t afford any more setbacks. So, whether it’s his next start or being pushed back or whatever it is, we’ve got to make sure that he comes out ready to go in the postseason.”
Finally, right-hander and presumed closer Edwin Díaz doesn't appear to be making much progress amid his return from another injured list stint. Manager Dave Roberts, among others, was not happy with the results of his rehab outing over the weekend, and knows that at this moment, Díaz is not someone a World Series favorite wants in their bullpen this postseason.
Díaz had a slightly better outing Wednesday (one scoreless inning) after his disastrous Sunday performance of five earned runs in 0.2 innings.
Here’s more information on these stories and all the latest Dodgers news (click the headline for the full article):
Dodgers Tweets of the Day
Sign up for our free newsletter and follow us on X/Twitter and Facebook for the latest news.
Gabe Smallson is a sportswriter based in Los Angeles with a focus in sports and entertainment content. Gabe has previously worked at Newsweek and Dodgers Nation. He graduated from San Francisco State University in 2020 and received his Masters of Science at the University of Southern California in 2025.

item.title: [FanSided] Ranking the most important Dodgers who could come back for the MLB Playoffs
item.dc:creator: Christopher Kline
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers are on track to win the NL West and probably earn a first-round bye in the postseason. That comes despite a recent onslaught of injuries. Los Angeles is not unaccustomed to a stacked injury list, but the Dodgers' elite depth — aided by a top-ranked farm system and unrivalred spending power — makes them uniquely resilient. What has helped L.A. win back-to-back World Series titles, however, is their knack for getting healthy at the right time and charging into October at fu
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are on track to win the NL West and probably earn a first-round bye in the postseason. That comes despite a recent onslaught of injuries. Los Angeles is not unaccustomed to a stacked injury list, but the Dodgers' elite depth — aided by a top-ranked farm system and unrivalred spending power — makes them uniquely resilient.
What has helped L.A. win back-to-back World Series titles, however, is their knack for getting healthy at the right time and charging into October at full strength. The Dodgers are hoping to do just that, again. Let's rank six potential returners who could make an outsized impact.
6. RHP Edwin Díaz
Should Edwin Díaz actually come back for the playoffs? He got rocked in his recent Triple-A rehab appearance. The Dodgers' prized $69 million investment has only pitched 13.2 innings in the majors this season, with a disastrous 11.85 ERA (not a typo). Díaz has not looked right at any point.
While the Dodgers presumably want such an expensive and accomplished reliever on the postseason roster, it may be smarter to punt on this season entirely. Díaz is more than capable of rebuilding confidence and getting healthy in the offseason, but it's unclear if L.A. can rely on him in even the lowest-leverage spots currently. Rather than playing with fire, so to speak, the Dodgers should probably lean on their spectacular bullpen depth and keep Díaz on the sidelines. The risk far outweighs the potential reward of rushing him back.
That said, when healthy, Díaz has a long track record as one of MLB's best closers. We know he can electify in the late innings. If the Dodgers are confident for reasons we on the outside aren't privy too, never say never on a triumphant turnaround.
5. RHP Roki Sasaki
Through two seasons, the Rōki Sasaki experience has not quite lived up to expectations for Dodgers fans. Hailed as the best Japanese pitching prospect in a generation, the 24-year-old looks an awful lot like... a prospect. A work in progress. Los Angeles expected immediate results. Now, the Dodgers are hoping Sasaki can iron out command issues against MLB competition. He appeared briefly in the minors this season, but the Dodgers are effectively all-in on Sasaki as a major league pitcher.
Sasaki is expected to recover from a blister before the playoffs, although the Dodgers are uncertain about his exact role. The rotation is much too deep for Sasaki to start in a must-win environment. He was effectively L.A.'s closer last October — a role in which he thrived — but a healthy Tanner Scott removes Sasaki from consideration for that role. Expect him in the bullpen, probably handling bulk work if one of L.A.'s starters is forced out early.
4. C Dalton Rushing
Dalton Rushing was recently returned to the IL after suffering a setback in his recovery from UCL surgery. He's done catching for the season, but L.A. still hopes the 25-year-old can return as a hitter. Of course, if Rushing is effectively relegated to DH, it will be hard to get him in the lineup with Shohei Ohtani also on the roster. Rushing could end up as a situational, pinch-hitter type in October, if he's even on the roster.
It's a credit to how deep the Dodgers are that Rushing being "situational," rather than essential, is even in the cards. The rookie backstop cooled off after the All-Star break, but he's still phenomenally talented. He has a .798 OPS and 120 wRC+ as a rookie, with 12 home runs in only 250 at-bats.
Rushing is stuck behind Will Smith on the org chart, which complicates his future somewhat, but the Dodgers will find ways to use him if he's available.
3. RHP Edgardo Henriquez
The Dodgers hope Edgardo Henriquez can return from a low-grade back strain come the playoffs. The 24-year-old fireballer has quickly established himself as one of baseball's most dominant relievers. He has a 2.85 ERA and 1.03 WHIP with 71 strikeouts in 60.0 innings pitched this season; he ranks in MLB's 99th percentile for both hard-hit rate (27.1 percent) and average fastball velo (100.8 mph).
Henriquez is more than a hard-thrower. He misses barrels and limits explosive hits, able to force groundballs or lifeless bloopers just as often as he forces swing-and-miss. He leans heavily on his four-seam and sinker combo, with a sweeping slider that leaves opposing hitters gasping for air (.191 xwOBA). Should Henriquez return in time, the Dodgers can plug him right into high-leverage spots and expect results. He's the real deal, folks.
2. OF Andy Pages
Andy Pages is back in the batting cage after breaking his hand in mid-August. The Dodgers' centerfielder has enjoyed a proper breakout campaign, posting a .797 OPS and 119 wRC+ with elite defensive metrics and 12 stolen bases. In terms of fWAR, or wins above replacement, Pages ranks third among L.A. positional players (3.9), behind only Shohei Ohtani (6.8) and Max Muncy (4.0).
The Dodgers really need Pages on cleanup duty in centerfield. He covers so much ground and features a killer arm, which wipes runs off the board. Pages' bat cooled down before the injury, but he's still far more dangerous than L.A.'s alternatives — although the recent promotion of top prospect Josue De Paula does create a difficult decision for manager Dave Roberts, assuming the DH spot reverts back to Ohtani.
Speaking of which...
1. DH Shohei Ohtani
This was obvious, yeah? Shohei Ohtani is currently on ice as he attempts to shed bicep and knee problems. That said, the Dodgers plan to get him back before the regular season ends — and it would be absolutely shocking if Ohtani weren't leading off in Game 1 of the Dodgers' first postseason series.
The nagging nature of Ohtani's injuries mean he won't take the mound again in 2026, but he's still the most valuable hitter in the majors, on balance. Yes, Yordan Álvarez and Pete Crow-Armstrong are enjoying better seasons, but Ohtani is the man you want at the plate in a big spot. Drafting a fantasy team, he's your No. 1 pick. So on and so forth.
After spending the early portion of his MLB career on an unserious Angels team, Ohtani is two-for-two in the World Series since joining the Dodgers. He has consistently come up large in the playoffs. Assuming Ohtani is anywhere close to 100 percent, the Dodgers are once again (easy) favorites to win it all.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Dodgers Make Kyle Tucker Playoff Roster Decision After $240 Million Disappointment
item.dc:creator: Peter Chawaga; Contributor
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers have a difficult decision ahead as they prepare for the postseason, and it could mean a harsh end for a star offseason acquisition. With All-Star reliever Edwin Diaz struggling to earn his way back into the bullpen following an injury, the team has indicated that he won't be guaranteed a spot on the playoff roster. item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers have a difficult decision ahead as they prepare for the postseason, and it could mean a harsh end for a star offseason acquisition.
With All-Star reliever Edwin Diaz struggling to earn his way back into the bullpen following an injury, the team has indicated that he won't be guaranteed a spot on the playoff roster.
"All-Star closer Edwin Díaz continues to struggle, as Tanner Scott did a year ago, and his rehab assignment with Triple-A Oklahoma City has gone poorly enough that Dodgers manager Dave Roberts acknowledged Monday the club could leave the three-time All-Star closer off the postseason roster," Fabian Ardaya wrote for The Athletic.
That uncertainty creates an obvious question about another high-profile Dodgers addition who has struggled throughout his first season in Los Angeles: Kyle Tucker.
The four-time All-Star signed a four-year, $240 million contract with the Dodgers during the offseason, but his production has fallen well short of what the team presumably expected when it made that investment.
Los Angeles Dodgers Send Definitive Kyle Tucker Message With Playoffs Looming
Though the Dodgers' willingness to leave Diaz off of the postseason roster suggests the team is evaluating performance alone, Roberts sent a clear message about any upcoming roster decisions involving Tucker.
"I told him, I'm gonna ride or die with him," Roberts said, according to the New York Post's Jack Harris.
That commitment comes despite a season in which Tucker has produced a .226/.327/.374 slash line with 15 home runs and 66 RBI through 143 games, soliciting calls that he be benched or platooned, if not removed from the upcoming playoff roster altogether. His performance has also been dramatically different at home than it has been on the road. Tucker has hit .187 with a .572 OPS at Dodger Stadium, compared with a .266 average and .826 OPS away from home.
That split adds another layer to the pressure surrounding Tucker as the Dodgers move toward the postseason.
$240 Million Los Angeles Dodgers Disappointment Brings Kyle Tucker Playoff Question Into Focus
Roberts' definitive commitment is particularly notable given how disappointing his first season has been relative to his contract.
"At this point, it is all adding up to a lost season for the 29-year-old, who is threatening to become one of the biggest free-agent flops in at least the sport's recent high-priced history," Harris added. "And yet, the Dodgers aren't wavering from their commitment to keep playing the four-time All-Star, rolling the dice 'talent level' and 'proven track record,' as Roberts cited, by keeping him in the lineup for the long haul."
That gives Tucker a clear path to remain part of the Dodgers' postseason plans, even as the club evaluates other difficult roster decisions.
This article was originally published on Forbes.com

item.title: [Orange County Register] Dodgers’ Roki Sasaki throws simulated game – but what role awaits him?
item.dc:creator: Bill Plunkett
item.description: CINCINNATI — Now what? Roki Sasaki threw 48 pitches in four simulated innings to Dodgers hitters on Wednesday afternoon, testing the blister on his right hand that landed him on the injured list. He gave up a home run to Eliezer Alfonzo but otherwise “was good,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said. Sasaki threw with Dermabond on his injured finger. A surgical adhesive used to close cuts and incisions, pitchers are allowed to use it in games if their team gets permission from MLB in advance. “He ca
item.content:encoded:
CINCINNATI — Now what?
Roki Sasaki threw 48 pitches in four simulated innings to Dodgers hitters on Wednesday afternoon, testing the blister on his right hand that landed him on the injured list. He gave up a home run to Eliezer Alfonzo but otherwise “was good,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said.
Sasaki threw with Dermabond on his injured finger. A surgical adhesive used to close cuts and incisions, pitchers are allowed to use it in games if their team gets permission from MLB in advance.
“He came out of it well,” Roberts said. “So we have to huddle up here and figure out what’s his role. What does it look like as we sit here on the 17th or 18th of September, whatever? So the number one most important thing is that he came out of that session well, and then now we got to figure out how to plug him in. He’s going to be important, but I just don’t know right now what role.”
Sasaki seemed destined for a bullpen role again this postseason, a role he assumed successfully last year. But the Dodgers have reason to hesitate on turning Sasaki into a reliever with Blake Snell leaving his start after just one inning on Wednesday night and Tyler Glasnow’s status.
Glasnow flew back to Los Angeles after his start in Miami. It was the second consecutive start in which Glasnow was not sharp and this time he could be seen in the dugout stretching out his back. But after the game, he said his back felt fine and Roberts said Glasnow threw a “normal” bullpen session in L.A. on Wednesday and is scheduled to make his next start on Friday night.
Sasaki is penciled in now to start during the series against the San Diego Padres in Los Angeles next week and remain a starter at least for now.
“One can argue it’s best to take down a couple starts, keep him built up, because if something does happen, he’s built up,” Roberts said. “The other side is you can assimilate him into the ’pen and get comfortable in that role – if that is the role.
“But again, I don’t want to speak out of turn and say that’s done, because it’s not.”
NO SHO
The Dodgers are about to complete their first road trip in three seasons without Shohei Ohtani. Yoshinobu Yamamoto might have missed Ohtani more than any other of his teammates.
“It’s been a weird feeling because I talk to him all the time in the clubhouse,” Yamamoto joked through his interpreter when asked about Ohtani’s absence. “All I have is Roki, but he doesn’t really talk to me.”
Back in Los Angeles, Ohtani has been receiving treatment for his knee and bicep injuries. According to Roberts, Ohtani began swinging a bat, hitting off a tee this week.
“There’s going to be a consistent build-up,” Roberts said. “Don’t know when the time of return to play is, but today was positive, and hopefully we can just keep building towards that.”
Ohtani will be eligible to be activated from the IL next Wednesday. Whether he is ready to play that day or shortly after, Roberts said the expectation is that Ohtani will return in time to play before the regular season ends on Sept. 27.
“I do,” Roberts said. “Whether it happens or not is to be determined. But I do expect him to be back to play in some regular-season games. Don’t know how many of them.”
COMING/GOING
Right-hander Edwin Diaz made his fifth rehab appearance with Triple-A Oklahoma City on Wednesday, pitching a scoreless inning to close out the Comets’ playoff berth-clinching victory. Diaz did allow a double to a fellow big-leaguer on rehab, Miguel Andujar.
Meanwhile, Edgardo Henriquez returned to Los Angeles and underwent an MRI, which confirmed the diagnosis of a “low-grade back strain,” Roberts said. He won’t be eligible to pitch again in the regular season but Roberts said the Dodgers are “hopeful” he could come back for the postseason.
Left-hander Kris Bubic was activated from the 60-day IL before Wednesday’s game and right-hander Paul Gervase was returned to OKC. In order to clear a spot on the 40-man roster for Bubic, Triple-A outfielder Ryan Ward was designated for assignment.
Right-hander Landon Knack will be added to the active roster before Thursday’s game and Bobby Miller will be returned to OKC.
ALSO
Outfield prospect Charles Davalan (the 41st pick in last year’s draft) was named MVP of the Class-A Midwest League and Great Lakes manager Jair Fernandez was named the league’s Manager of the Year. Davalan hit .292 with 24 home runs and a .937 OPS. He is scheduled to play in the Arizona Fall League, where he is expected to start testing out a possible conversion to second base.
UP NEXT
Dodgers (LHP Justin Wrobleski, 11-5, 3.78 ERA) at Reds (RHP Brady Singer, 6-14, 5.38 ERA), Thursday, 9:40 a.m., SportsNet LA, 570 AM

item.title: [New York Post] Blake Snell departs early and Dodgers’ rotation suddenly a question mark
item.dc:creator: Dylan Hernandez
item.description: Shohei Ohtani’s aching right arm. Freddie Freeman’s throbbing right knee. Edwin Díaz’s disastrous form on a minor-league rehabilitation assignment. Whatever problems surfaced in recent weeks, the Dodgers were able to convince themselves they could overcome them. The reason: Even with Ohtani unable to pitch, they had the most talented starting rotation of this era. Suddenly, that source of comfort is a major concern. Blake Snell departed his start in Cincinnati on Wednesday after just one inning
item.content:encoded:
Shohei Ohtani’s aching right arm. Freddie Freeman’s throbbing right knee. Edwin Díaz’s disastrous form on a minor-league rehabilitation assignment.
Whatever problems surfaced in recent weeks, the Dodgers were able to convince themselves they could overcome them.
The reason: Even with Ohtani unable to pitch, they had the most talented starting rotation of this era.
Suddenly, that source of comfort is a major concern.
Blake Snell departed his start in Cincinnati on Wednesday after just one inning with what was described as a tight left groin.
Consider that Tyler Glasnow traveled directly home from Miami rather than to follow the Dodgers to Great American Ball Park for their four-game series against the Reds, and there are reasons to be worried.
Very worried.
With an inconsistent offense and combustible bullpen, the Dodgers were going to be heavily dependent on their starting pitching in the playoffs.
That rotation could now be unraveling.
Download The California Post App, follow us on social, and subscribe to our newsletters
California Post News: Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, X, YouTube, WhatsApp, LinkedIn
California Post Sports Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, X
California Post Opinion
California Post Newsletters: Sign up here!
California Post App: Download here!
Home delivery: Sign up here!
Page Six Hollywood: Sign up here!
The last time Snell strained his left groin was when he was pitching for the San Francisco Giants in 2024. He was sidelined for a month.
For what it’s worth, Snell is convinced this particular injury isn’t severe and plans to make his next start, according to people familiar with this situation.
“Stopped before it got too bad,” one of the people said.
Then again, weren’t similar claims once made about Ohtani?
As for Glasnow, he remains on track to pitch on Friday.
Manager Dave Roberts said Glasnow skipped the Cincinnati leg of the trip to better prepare for his starting assignment at Dodger Stadium against the San Francisco Giants.
“Get him acclimated to Pacific Standard Time,” Roberts said.
By sending Glasnow back to Los Angeles, the Dodgers spared him a three-hour flight from Miami to Cincinnati.
Glasnow was sidelined for 3 ½ months because of back problems, and Roberts intimated something could be wrong with him after his most recent start. In his last two appearances, the 6-foot-8 right-hander gave up a combined eight runs, 11 hits and seven walks in 10 innings.
The questions about Snell’s and Glasnow’s health came at a time when the rotation was coming together before the postseason.
Snell in particular was sharp after returning from an elbow cleanup that cost him three months. Before his early departure on Wednesday, Snell was 4-0 with a 1.04 earned-run average since he was activated from the injured list on Aug. 11.
Snell wasn’t the only Cy Young Award-caliber pitcher rounding into shape.
The day before Snell scaled the mound, it was Yamamoto’s turn to do so, and last year’s World Series Most Valuable Player pitched seven scoreless innings in a 4-0 win over the Reds.
The seven-inning start was the third in a row for Yamamoto, who improved his record to 14-8 and lowered his earned-run average to 2.51.
“I feel really good and I don’t have any physical problems,” Yamamoto told reporters in Japanese. “I want to treat practice each and every day with importance and go into October in the best condition.”
The opening game of the series was started by Tarik Skubal, the two-time Cy Young Award winner who was acquired from the Detroit Tigers before the trade deadline.
Skubal pitched seven scoreless innings of his own in a 4-1 victory over the Reds. In his previous start, which was also against the Reds but at Dodger Stadium, Skubal pitched 7 ⅓ innings.
“Just getting in a rhythm,” Skubal said.
Just last week, the Dodgers had a playoff rotation that would have looked to other teams like the Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse.
Now, there’s a chance they could be forced to send Roki Sasaki and Emmet Sheehan to the mound in playoff games.
The Dodgers could conceivably win a championship with a rotation of Yamamoto, Skubal, Sasaki and Sheehan but that would require their offense to be productive.
How much can the Dodgers count on that, considering the physical problems Ohtani and Freeman have encountered? And how would using Sasaki as a starter instead of a reliever affect their bullpen?
Snell removed himself from his start on Wednesday so the Dodgers wouldn’t have to find out. The question is whether he did so in time. Their season depends on it.

item.title: [Claro Sports] Edwin Díaz, bajo presión: ¿podría perder su lugar con los Dodgers?
item.dc:creator: Julian Castillo
item.description: La irregularidad de Edwin Díaz abre la puerta a que Dodgers evalúe dejarlo fuera del roster para los playoffs. La presión crece alrededor de Edwin Díaz en un momento especialmente delicado para los Dodgers. El relevista boricua llegó a Los Ángeles con el cartel de cerrador élite y con un contrato de tres años y $69 millones de dólares, una inversión diseñada para reforzar el último inning de un bullpen que había dejado dudas durante 2025. Sin embargo, su primera temporada en Dodger Stadium se ha
item.content:encoded:
La irregularidad de Edwin Díaz abre la puerta a que Dodgers evalúe dejarlo fuera del roster para los playoffs.
La presión crece alrededor de Edwin Díaz en un momento especialmente delicado para los Dodgers. El relevista boricua llegó a Los Ángeles con el cartel de cerrador élite y con un contrato de tres años y $69 millones de dólares, una inversión diseñada para reforzar el último inning de un bullpen que había dejado dudas durante 2025. Sin embargo, su primera temporada en Dodger Stadium se ha alejado de ese plan.
Díaz ha tenido problemas para encontrar consistencia, salud y comando. En 16 apariciones con los Dodgers registra una efectividad de 11.85, con 18 carreras limpias permitidas en 13 innings y dos tercios, además de cuatro salvamentos desperdiciados en 11 oportunidades. En 2025, todavía con los Mets, había firmado una efectividad de 1.63 y solo había dejado escapar tres rescates en 31 oportunidades.
El panorama se volvió aún más complejo después de su última aparición en Grandes Ligas, el 17 de agosto ante los Rockies de Colorado. Díaz permitió tres carreras en un inning, con cuatro hits recibidos, y al día siguiente ingresó a la lista de lesionados por inflamación en el cuello. Ahora continúa en Triple-A con los Oklahoma City Comets, donde busca recuperar ritmo, ajustar su mecánica y convencer al club de que puede aportar en la recta final.
MÁS INFORMACIÓN: Edwin Díaz tuvo una salida perfecta en el triunfo agónico de los Dodgers sobre los Royals
Edwin Díaz enfrenta una presión inesperada con Dodgers
El foco está en su lugar dentro del bullpen y, más concretamente, en la posibilidad de que no llegue a ocupar nuevamente el noveno inning ni entre al roster de postemporada.
Para un pitcher de su trayectoria, la situación resulta poco habitual. Díaz fue uno de los relevistas más cotizados del último mercado de agentes libres y los Dodgers lo firmaron para aportar experiencia, ponches y seguridad en los juegos cerrados. Su llegada respondía a una necesidad clara del equipo, que buscaba una figura estable para cerrar los partidos de alto voltaje.
Los resultados, no obstante, han obligado a Los Ángeles a manejar el caso con cautela. Su recta ha perdido velocidad en comparación con temporadas anteriores y su ángulo de brazo bajó de un promedio de 19 grados en 2025 a 15 grados durante esta campaña. Esa modificación ha afectado tanto su ubicación como la efectividad de sus pitcheos, especialmente una recta que ya no genera los mismos swings fallidos.
El problema no se limita a los números. Díaz pasó cerca de tres meses fuera tras someterse a una cirugía artroscópica para retirarle cuerpos libres del codo derecho. Volvió a finales de julio, pero apenas pudo disputar algunos juegos antes de que la inflamación en el cuello lo enviara de regreso a la lista de lesionados.
Los Dodgers evalúan el roster de playoffs
De acuerdo con Ken Rosenthal, no sería descabellado que los Dodgers excluyan a Díaz de su roster de postemporada, incluso con el peso de su contrato. El razonamiento dentro de la organización sería simple, aunque duro para un relevista de su estatus. En octubre, Los Ángeles necesita llevar a sus mejores brazos disponibles, no necesariamente a los de mayor salario o trayectoria.
Dave Roberts también reconoció públicamente que Díaz necesita mostrar señales claras antes de recuperar un sitio asegurado. El manager mantiene confianza en el talento del puertorriqueño, pero ha dejado claro que el equipo necesita evidencia de que puede competir en situaciones de alta exigencia. Esa frase resume el momento del cerrador, que ya no tiene el puesto garantizado por historial ni por contrato.
La decisión tampoco se explica únicamente por la irregularidad de Díaz. Los Dodgers cuentan con alternativas en el bullpen y Tanner Scott ha asumido buena parte de las oportunidades de salvamento durante la ausencia del boricua. Scott ha convertido 21 de 24 chances de rescate y se ha establecido como la opción más frecuente para el noveno episodio.
Además,la organización ha sumado profundidad con el zurdo Kris Bubic, adquirido en la fecha límite de cambios. Bubic viene de una sólida rehabilitación, con cinco innings y dos tercios sin carreras y nueve ponches, una incorporación que amplía las variantes de Roberts para octubre.
MÁS INFORMACIÓN: Dodgers se desploman en Arizona: suman siete derrotas consecutivas
Oklahoma City será una prueba decisiva
La estadía de Díaz con los Oklahoma City Comets no es un trámite. Cada salida en Triple-A tiene valor en su intento por regresar a las Grandes Ligas. Aunque tuvo actuaciones sin carreras en sus primeras apariciones de rehabilitación, su presentación más reciente encendió las alarmas al permitir cinco carreras, dos hits y tres boletos en apenas dos tercios de inning.
El desafío para Díaz pasa por recuperar el comando y confianza en su repertorio. La velocidad de su recta ha rondado las 96 millas por hora, una cifra que sigue siendo competitiva, pero menor a sus estándares. En Triple-A también se ha visto una búsqueda mecánica para elevar el ángulo de su brazo y devolverle mayor vida a sus lanzamientos.
Los Dodgers no necesitan que Díaz vuelva de inmediato a la función de cerrador. Su ruta más lógica sería regresar en apariciones de menor presión, acumular innings efectivos y demostrar que puede ser una opción fiable. El contrato de $69 millones de dólares no garantiza un lugar cuando el equipo se prepara para la etapa más importante del año.

item.title: [Dodgers Nation] Edwin Diaz Makes His Case After Dave Roberts Questions Postseason Role

But it’s like, where we’re at, there’s got to be something for us to be
item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers reliever Edwin Diaz responded to manager Dave Roberts’ postseason warning with a better outing.
Roberts was asked Monday about Diaz’s concerning Triple-A performance. He has a 12.46 ERA over 4.1 innings in his current rehab assignment due to neck inflammation.
The manager didn’t mince words about Diaz’s postseason status.
“He needs to pitch better. I think the world of him. The baseball card looks great. But it’s like, where we’re at, there’s got to be something for us to be able to hang our hat on. And he knows that. He knows that. He wants to pitch well,” Roberts said.
Diaz’s most concerning outing came on Sunday, when he allowed two hits, three walks, and hit a batter, allowing a total of five runs.
On Wednesday, Diaz came out to the challenge Roberts posed to improve his final line and delivered a promising outing.
He allowed one hit, a 100+ mph double, according to Baseball Savant, along with two flyouts and a groundout.
Diaz had no whiffs, which is certainly concerning for a pitcher known for swing-and-miss stuff.
On the bright side, Diaz averaged 1.6 MPH more on his fastball, and he had more induced vertical break on the slider, adding another two inches from his season average.
Where does Edwin Diaz go from here?
The OKC Comets have four games left on their schedule, meaning Diaz could make two more appearances before he needs to return to the Dodgers for additional action.
At that point, Diaz will get some chances to show the Dodgers why he should be on the playoff roster.
“We have to go with our best pitchers, as far as performance, talent, all that stuff,” Roberts said.
“So my bet is that he will be (on the roster). But again, there’s got to be some kind of evidence or something for us, again, to sort of bet on. And so my bet is yes, but we still got to see something.”
Diaz’s reputation can take him far and give him the nod in a bullpen with some other question marks, but it will ultimately come down to his final outings for the Dodgers.

item.title: [The Big Lead] Dodgers pitcher who touched 104 mph might be done for the season
item.dc:creator: J P Hoornstra

Bill Plunkett of the Southern California News Group reported Wednesday, Sept. 16, that the pitcher is “hopeful” he can return in October after getting the results of an MRI exam. “Hopeful”
item.content:encoded:
Edgardo Henriquez’s regular season was already effectively over once the Dodgers placed the hard-throwing pitcher on the 15-day injured list Monday with low back discomfort.
Henriquez, whose 103.6-mph fastball was the fastest pitch thrown by a Dodger since at least 2008, was diagnoesed with a low back strain. Bill Plunkett of the Southern California News Group reported Wednesday, Sept. 16, that the pitcher is “hopeful” he can return in October after getting the results of an MRI exam.
“Hopeful” and “probable” can be a world apart. In Henriquez’s case, it’s unclear whether his hope stems from the severity of his diagnosis, or from his faith that the Dodgers will play deep enough into the postseason to give him a chance to recover.
In either event, the Dodgers’ bullpen without Henriquez is a very different one than what they hoped to carry in their quest to three-peat as World Series champions.
Henriquez’s fastball touched 103.6 on June 2 in a game against the Arizona Diamondbacks, and again on Aug. 29 in a game against the Detroit Tigers.
Speed is just one facet of Henriquez’s game. His 71-to-25 strikeout-to-walk ratio, combined with only 37 hits allowed in 60 innings, gave the right-hander an at-times untouchable arsenal.
No right-handed pitcher had made more appearances for the Dodgers this season than Henriquez’s 61. Without him, manager Dave Roberts might have to get creative.
Right-hander Roki Sasaki, a starter during the regular season and a reliever during the team’s 2025 World Series run, might return in a relief role once he’s recovered from a finger blister. Edwin Diaz, who is currently on a rehab assignment of his own, struggled mightily in the closer’s role this season — but might be needed in some capacity just to get the Dodgers through to the end of the postseason.
Diaz, a three-time All-Star, had an 11.85 ERA in 16 appearances with the Dodgers before landing on the injured list with a neck injury Aug. 16.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Edgardo Henriquez Gets Positive MRI, Dodgers Hopeful for Postseason Return
item.dc:creator: Nelson Espinal

Henriquez has a "low-grade" back strain, and the team is "hopeful" he'll be back for the postseason, manager Dave Roberts said. Roberts described the MRI results as "positive," which should be a relief for fans hoping to get their best bullpen arm back in time for the playoffs. The Dodgers placed him on the 15-day injured list, meaning that he is not eligible
item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers key reliever Edgardo Henriquez got the official diagnosis for his lower-body injury that has him on the injured list.
Henriquez has a "low-grade" back strain, and the team is "hopeful" he'll be back for the postseason, manager Dave Roberts said.
Roberts described the MRI results as "positive," which should be a relief for fans hoping to get their best bullpen arm back in time for the playoffs.
The Dodgers placed him on the 15-day injured list, meaning that he is not eligible to return until September 29th, effectively ending his regular season.
All eyes will be on Henriquez as we look toward October, when he is expected to be a high-leverage arm, possibly even the closer if he is able to get back to pitching again soon.
Why Henriquez is so important for the Dodgers
Henriquez has a 2.62 ERA, with a 2.50 FIP. He misses the barrel of the bat, strikes out hitters, and limits home runs like one of the best relievers.
He throws triple digits, which may explain his back issue, but the pitch's movement and growing command make it a deadly weapon out of the bullpen.
While he lacks the high-leverage experience of players like Edwin Diaz and Tanner Scott, Henriquez carries himself confidently and exudes a strong presence whenever he takes the mound.
It is unclear how quickly the Dodgers will pull the trigger on Henriquez in the playoffs for a high-leverage role, but given what he has proven this year, they will try to lean on him as much as his health permits.

Henriquez’s injury was initially labeled as lower back discomfort. With further imaging and testing, Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said the injury is a “low-grade back strain,” per MLB.com’s Sonja Chen. Although Edgardo Henriquez’s regular season is over, he still remains someone that Los Angeles can get back for the p
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers will be without relief pitcher Edgardo Henriquez for the remainder of the regular season. The 24-year-old was placed on the 15-day injured list on Sept. 14.
Henriquez’s injury was initially labeled as lower back discomfort. With further imaging and testing, Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said the injury is a “low-grade back strain,” per MLB.com’s Sonja Chen.
Although Edgardo Henriquez’s regular season is over, he still remains someone that Los Angeles can get back for the postseason. Dave Roberts said that he remains “hopeful” that Henriquez can return in October.
Edgardo Henriquez’s Dominant 2026 Season
Coming off limited MLB experience, Edgardo Henriquez displayed the best pitching of his career in 2026. The high-velocity right-handed pitcher was a reliable piece of the Dodgers’ bullpen throughout the season.
In 61 appearances, Henriquez finished with a 4-1 record, 2.85 ERA, and 1.03 WHIP across 60.0 innings pitched. He also added 11 holds and two saves in the season.
Henriquez was among the hardest-throwing pitchers in the league. The 24-year-old’s fastball reached as fast as 104 miles per hour this season.
“He hit 103 mph or higher 17 times, more than any Major League pitcher not named Jacob Misiorowski (140 pitches) or Mason Miller (33 pitches). But Henriquez became more than just a hard thrower this year, developing the command and the confidence to be a leverage weapon for the Dodgers,” MLB.com’s Sonja Chen wrote.
Dodgers Still Searching For Answers on Edwin Diaz’s Status
The Los Angeles Dodgers made closer Edwin Diaz the most expensive reliever in MLB last offseason, signing him to a three-year, $69 million contract.
Diaz’s first season with the Dodgers has not been what many expected. While dealing with injuries, Diaz’s season stats include a 2-2 record, 11.85 ERA, and 2.56 WHIP across 13.2 innings pitched.
While dealing with inflammation in his neck, Edwin Diaz has remained on the injured list since Aug. 18. He has since begun a rehab assignment, with results that haven’t gone well.
The 32-year-old allowed five runs in a rehab appearance in Triple-A Oklahoma City on Sept. 13. Dave Roberts says that if Diaz’s game doesn’t improve, he could be left off the Dodgers’ postseason roster, according to The Athletic’s Fabian Ardaya.
“He needs to pitch better,” Roberts also mentioned. “I think the world of him. The baseball card looks great. But it’s like, where we’re at, there’s got to be something for us to be able to hang our hat on. And he knows that.”
Diaz made another rehab appearance on Wednesday, pitching one scoreless inning. However, he didn’t produce a swing-and-miss and gave up a double, says Ardaya.

item.title: [Los Angeles Times] Shohei Ohtani, Carlos Correa and more: How star injuries could reshape the MLB playoffs
item.dc:creator: Steve Henson
item.description: - Click here to listen to this article - - As October approaches, injuries and recoveries are poised to reshape the MLB postseason picture, with nearly every contender juggling critical absences and fragile returns. - Houston shuts down Carlos Correa after an ankle setback, the Yankees finally get Max Fried and Aaron Judge back, while Shohei Ohtani looms as the Dodgers’ biggest question. Carlos Correa is out. Max Fried is back. Shohei Ohtani is somewhere in-between. And questions linger ov
item.content:encoded:
- Click here to listen to this article
-
- As October approaches, injuries and recoveries are poised to reshape the MLB postseason picture, with nearly every contender juggling critical absences and fragile returns.
- Houston shuts down Carlos Correa after an ankle setback, the Yankees finally get Max Fried and Aaron Judge back, while Shohei Ohtani looms as the Dodgers’ biggest question.
Carlos Correa is out. Max Fried is back. Shohei Ohtani is somewhere in-between. And questions linger over the postseason availability of several other MLB difference-makers as October approaches.
Here is a look at the injury status and hopeful returns of impact players on playoff qualifiers and contenders:
American League East
Tampa Bay Rays: Acquired from Baltimore at the trade deadline, swingman Tyler Wells posted a 1.50 earned-run-average before right forearm tightness sidelined him. He is back solely pitching from the bullpen, and could be a key piece for the Rays in their surprising surge to the division title.
Hopeful return: Slick-fielding shortstop Taylor Walls is recovering from a right hip flexor strain and signs point to him returning by October.
The Dodgers clinch a playoff berth with their 4-1 victory over the Cincinnati Reds, reaching the postseason for a record-tying 14th consecutive year.
New York Yankees: The return of staff ace Fried is huge for a team that has clinched a wild-card berth and remains a long step behind the Rays for a division title and first-round bye. The left-hander out of Studio City Harvard-Westlake High gave up one run while walking none over seven innings in his longest start in almost five months. Fried has had two arduous IL stints dealing with a bone bruise on his left elbow.
Hopeful returns: Giancarlo Stanton or Trent Grisham returning in October would give the Yankees lineup additional pop. Three-time AL MVP Aaron Judge has been back for a week since missing more than three months with a fractured rib.
Boston Red Sox: A right quadriceps strain has kept All-Star center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela sidelined for two weeks. However, Rafaela told NESN that he expects to be activated this weekend, a substantial addition to a team that likely will play the Yankees in wild-card series.
Hopeful return: A year ago, Garrett Crochet was 18-5 and led the AL with 205 1/3 innings pitched. This year, left shoulder inflammation and a lat strain have kept him sidelined since April. However, he has ramped up bullpen sessions and is targeting a postseason return as a reliever.
American League Central
Chicago White Sox: The most improved team in baseball is desperately trying to hold off the Guardians and win a division title after finishing last two years in a row. Chicago has enjoyed good health and added journeyman outfielder Tommy Pham from the Phillies on Aug. 31. Pham was activated from the IL on Wednesday and could provide valuable postseason experience to complement his young new teammates — he has hit .315 in 37 career playoff games.
Hopeful return: Drew Thorpe was reinstated from the 60-day IL on Wednesday and is an intriguing option. The right-hander from Cal Poly SLO was a key piece in the 2024 trade that sent Dylan Cease to the Padres but has spent nearly two full seasons on the shelf. Now healthy, his inclusion on the playoff roster would be a gamble that his elite stuff can mask his inexperience.
Cleveland Guardians: Jo Adell didn’t come off the IL, but the addition of the former confounding Angels prospect in an August salary dump has bolstered the Guardians’ outfield — long a problem area. Adell has driven in 28 runs in 38 games with Cleveland and joins glittering rookie Chase DeLauter and steady veteran Steven Kwan in a productive outfield.
Hopeful return: Reliever Shawn Armstrong, who signed a one-year, $5.5 million contract last offseason, has been sidelined since July 24 with a calf strain. Barring a setback in his final minor league rehab appearance, he could be activated in time for the playoffs.
American League West
Houston Astros: Correa, whose second act with Houston has been a flop because of injuries, was working on an accelerated comeback from May ankle surgery. A few days ago team officials expressed optimism, but Tuesday they decided to shelve their shortstop when the ankle became inflamed after a workout. Houston is clinging to a one-game lead over the Texas Rangers in the AL West.
Hopeful return: Nothing of note.
Texas Rangers: Still in contention despite spending much of the season under .500, the Rangers welcomed back pitcher Nathan Eovaldi and third baseman Josh Jung from the injured list over the weekend. A calf strain had kept Jung sidelined since July 21 and Eovaldi had been out since Aug. 7 with elbow inflammation. Eovaldi, who has started in all but 20 of his 339 MLB appearances, will pitch out of the bullpen.
Hopeful return: Nothing of note
National League East
Atlanta Braves: Reynaldo López inflated hopes of a late-career surge when he posted a 1.99 ERA over 25 starts in his first season with Atlanta. But injuries — including right shoulder inflammation this season — have severely limited his contribution. López was placed on the IL again Tuesday.
Hopeful return: Bryce Elder had an arthroscopic procedure to clean up bone fragments in his right knee on Sept. 8. The hope is that the right-handed starter can recover quickly enough to be counted upon in the postseason.
By not putting Shohei Ohtani on the injured list in July or in August, the Dodgers may have compromised the two-way star’s ability to be healthy for the playoffs.
Philadelphia Phillies: Although an MRI found no structural damage to the throwing shoulder of stalwart starter Jesús Luzardo, the left-hander remains a question for the playoffs. He was placed on the 15-day IL retroactive to Sept. 12, and it is doubtful he could pitch again in the regular season. Luzardo has a 2.87 ERA across 29 starts this season.
Hopeful return: Tanner Banks, a major contributor to the Philadelphia bullpen in 2025, was reinstated from the 60-day IL over the weekend. Although he wasn’t effective earlier this season, Banks is welcomed back because Phillies relievers have been poor against left-handed hitters.
National League Central
Milwaukee Brewers: Huntington Beach Marina High product Jake Bauers has suffered from shin splints almost all season, and the pain has kept him from playing the outfield lately. He can play first base, but that takes slugger Andrew Vaughn out of the lineup. Bauers, with 26 home runs and 83 RBIs, has been a key bat for Milwaukee. He has been particularly tough against the Dodgers, batting .348 with a .483 on-base percentage.
Hopeful return: Brandon Woodruff, one of the best starters in baseball when healthy, is rehabbing from shoulder inflammation that sidelined him in July. The Brewers are nearly guaranteed a first-round bye, giving Woodruff an extra week to build stamina.
Chicago Cubs: Shortstop and team leader Dansby Swanson will be welcomed back after missing a month with a left oblique injury. He is expected to rejoin the Cubs during their weekend series against the Cincinnati Reds.
Hopeful return: Left-handed starter Justin Steele is progressing through bullpen sessions and is almost ready to take the mound after missing the entire season with a left elbow flexor strain. Steele, whose record was 16-5 in 2023, likely would pitch from the bullpen in the postseason.
National League West
Dodgers: The loss of center fielder Andy Pages is significant. He can bat near the top or bottom of the order, displays power and speed, and had improved his patience at the plate enough to earn a career-high 45 walks in 128 games.
Hopeful return: Getting Ohtani healthy enough to produce at the plate is a priority, and his absence from the mound shouldn’t be felt if Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell, Tarik Skubal and Tyler Glasnow pitch to their capabilities. Meanwhile, Edwin Diaz might not even make the playoff roster.
Edwin Díaz struggled in his rehab start Sunday, and Dave Roberts is making it clear the Dodgers “got to see something” before putting him on the playoff roster.
San Diego Padres: While recovering from Tommy John surgery, starter Joe Musgrove made it a goal to be ready for the postseason. Recovery difficulties between starts have made his status doubtful, however. Nick Pivetta, on the other hand, has pitched well in two starts since coming off the IL and appears ready.
Hopeful return: Ramón Laurenano, a 2025 trade deadline acquisition with a potent bat, last played May 30 because of hip inflammation. However, he told reporters that the chances of him playing in the postseason are “less than 5%.”
Arizona Diamondbacks: Zac Gallen was activated from the 60-day IL and Michael Soroka from the 15-day IL, giving the D-Backs two starters in their push to win a wild-card berth. Gallen, a proven starter who has been horrendous in 2026, has been out since the All-Star break with elbow inflammation. Soroka was out only two weeks with the same ailment.
Hopeful return: Third baseman Nolan Arenado suffered an injury to his left thumb Tuesday, the same injury he sustained in late August. It’s doubtful the injury would sideline the 14-year veteran with games this week being so important, yet the Diamondbacks have to hope the injury doesn’t impact his productivity.

item.title: [New York Post] Dodgers have glaring problems as playoffs approach — but also the threefold remedy
item.dc:creator: Dylan Hernandez
item.description: The Dodgers will be in every game they play in October, and that alone means they will enter the playoffs as the favorites to win the World Series. Not because of Shohei Ohtani. Not because of Freddie Freeman. And certainly not because of their bullpen. There were a number of alarming developments in the last week or so, but if any team is designed to survive them, it’s the Dodgers. Whatever their problems, they still have the best rotation in baseball. No player influences the outcome of a game
item.content:encoded:
The Dodgers will be in every game they play in October, and that alone means they will enter the playoffs as the favorites to win the World Series.
Not because of Shohei Ohtani. Not because of Freddie Freeman. And certainly not because of their bullpen.
There were a number of alarming developments in the last week or so, but if any team is designed to survive them, it’s the Dodgers.
Whatever their problems, they still have the best rotation in baseball.
No player influences the outcome of a game as much as a starting pitcher, and the Dodgers are the only team that will be able to roll out one Cy Young Award-caliber arm after another after another.
The Dodgers were negligent with Ohtani, and the verdict on their management of Freeman is pending, but they at least set up their pitchers the right way.
The rotation is more than a collection of big names. In Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal and Blake Snell, the Dodgers have three starters who are peaking in time to deliver the kinds of performances that will be required for them to win their third consecutive World Series.
Yoshinobu Yamamoto pitched seven shutout innings on Tuesday in a 4-0 win over the Cincinnati Reds, marking his third consecutive seven-inning start.
“I feel really good and I don’t have any physical problems,” Yamamoto told reporters in Japanese. “I want to treat practice each and every day with importance and go into October in the best condition.”
Yamamoto isn’t alone.
The day before Yamamoto’s start, Tarik Skubal pitched seven scoreless innings of his own in a 4-1 victory over the Reds. In his previous start, which was also against the Reds but at Dodger Stadium, Skubal pitched 7 ⅓ innings.
“Just getting in a rhythm,” Skubal said.
Blake Snell, who is scheduled to take his turn in the rotation on Wednesday, was 4-0 with a 1.04 earned-run average in the six games he started since returning from an elbow cleanup that cost him three months.
The one source of concern in the rotation is Tyler Glasnow, who, like Snell, was slow-played in his return from an injury. Sidelined for 3 ½ months because of back problems, Glasnow showed promise in his first couple of starts after he came back. But in his last two starts, he gave up a combined eight runs, 11 hits and seven walks in 10 innings. But as the team’s No. 4 starter, he is unlikely to start more than one game in any postseason series.
Even before Ohtani was placed on the injured list because of right arm and left knee injuries, the starting pitching was likely going to have to carry the Dodgers – much as it did last year.
Recent developments have shifted even more of the burden to the starting pitchers.
Edwin Diaz, their $69-million closer, was blow-torched for five runs in ⅔ of an inning in the most recent game of his minor-league rehabilitation assignment. At this point, he’s a longshot to make the postseason roster.
Diaz’s failure to rediscover his All-Star form will have major ramifications on the bullpen, which lost ninth-inning candidate Edgardo Henriquez to a lower-back problem for the remainder of the regular season. Henriquez’s status for the playoffs remains a mystery.
Manager Dave Roberts’ current ninth-inning choice, Tanner Scott, is in a minor slump, as he has given up runs in five of his last 12 apperances.
While the Dodgers will have to find a closer – Roki Sasaki? – their ability to create favorable matchups in the innings before the ninth is also under question. The simplest way to address those uncertainties will be for the starters to pitch deeper into games. Last year, Yamamoto pitched a complete game in the National League Championship Series and another in his next start in the World Series. Snell had an eight-inning start in the NLCS.
The greater problem could be the already-inconsistent offense, which could go into the playoffs with physically-compromised versions of Ohtani and Freeman.
Freeman missed three of five games before starting at first base on Tuesday. Freeman collected three hits in the game, but he’s 37 years old and the Dodgers can’t be certain how his right knee will hold up.
As for Ohtani, Roberts reported on Tuesday that he resumed baseball activities. Roberts said he expected Ohtani to return before the end of the regular season, but hedged his prediction.
“Whether it happens or not,” Roberts said, “is to be determined.”
If the Dodgers don’t know if Ohtani will be able to even step into the batter’s box next week, how could they possibly count on him to be a consistent source of offense?
They can’t.
In other words, the margin for error could be miniscule for the Dodgers. Their starting pitchers might have to be close to perfect. The challenge will be formidable. But considering who will be pitching for them, it will be very much in the realm of possibility.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Dodgers’ Kyle Tucker Signing Summed Up In 1 Painful Word
item.dc:creator: Billy Heyen
item.description: Everyone knew the Los Angeles Dodgers paid more to sign Kyle Tucker than anyone else in MLB was willing to pay. Even still, it seemed like the deal would be a good one for the back-to-back World Series champs. Tucker has been a multi-tool outfielder for his entire career, and now he'd be joined a stacked lineup that would, if anything, take some pressure off of him. It sure seemed like a no-brainer for everyone involved. Somehow, though, it has been a disaster. The Dodgers are still great, of co
item.content:encoded:
Everyone knew the Los Angeles Dodgers paid more to sign Kyle Tucker than anyone else in MLB was willing to pay.
Even still, it seemed like the deal would be a good one for the back-to-back World Series champs. Tucker has been a multi-tool outfielder for his entire career, and now he'd be joined a stacked lineup that would, if anything, take some pressure off of him.
It sure seemed like a no-brainer for everyone involved.
Somehow, though, it has been a disaster. The Dodgers are still great, of course, but Tucker hasn't contributed to that.
And so in an article earlier this week, ESPN's Bradford Doolittle summarized the disappointing signings of Tucker and closer Edwin Diaz in a single word:
"Ouch."
Yeah, that about sums it up.
Kyle Tucker Stats
Through Sept. 15, Tucker has played 143 games for the Dodgers. You've got to give him credit for showing up every day and trying to break out of a funk that seems never-ending.
For the season, he has batted just .226, though.
Tucker has slugged OK, at least, with 21 doubles, four triples and 15 home runs to give him a .701 OPS.
He also has stolen 11 bases without getting caught.
The problem is that Tucker signed a deal worth $60 million per year, and he's on pace for by far the lowest OPS of his career outside of a 28-game debut stint in 2018.
"The Dodgers' splash signings of Tucker and Edwin Diaz in last season's free agency were the cause of much handwringing about L.A.'s economic dominance," Doolittle writes. "While those high-level, targeted acquisitions looked like no-brainers at the time, the first year of both deals could hardly have gone worse. Together, Tucker and Diaz are at minus-1.0 bWAR for their Dodgers debuts while earning a combined $47 million. Ouch."
Tucker has homered twice in the last five games for the Dodgers, dating back to Sept. 11, so maybe it's a sign that he's heating up at just the right time.
It sure would be ironic if Tucker just coasted through a disappointing season but then stepped up in time to help them win the World Series again.
Edwin Diaz Stats
Diaz has dealt with injuries most of the season and is currently on the 15-day IL, but even when conceptually healthy, he's been rough.
In 16 outings, Diaz has an 11.86 ERA. He's allowed 18 runs (including three homers) in 13.1 innings. Diaz has also walked 10 guys, and while he's struck out 19, the punchouts haven't been enough to overcome the other issues.
At this point, it's not clear whether Diaz can be any kind of help down the stretch and into October.
The Dodgers rolled last postseason with a bullpen that relied on starting pitchers for the most part, and that may have to be the case again.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Kyle Tucker, Edwin Diaz Earn Title Nobody Wants for Dodgers
item.dc:creator: Ricardo Sandoval; Unknown
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers had yet another dream offseason in 2025-26. Diaz and Tucker signed lucrative contracts with the Dodgers; however, neither has panned out anywhere close to where the Dodgers had hoped. Instead, ESPN's Bradford Doolittle labeled the two as the biggest disappointment for the Dod
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers had yet another dream offseason in 2025-26.
The Dodgers were once again viewed as the winners of the offseason, earning the honor among media and fans for the third straight year after signing closer Edwin Diaz and star outfielder Kyle Tucker.
Diaz and Tucker signed lucrative contracts with the Dodgers; however, neither has panned out anywhere close to where the Dodgers had hoped.
Instead, ESPN's Bradford Doolittle labeled the two as the biggest disappointment for the Dodgers as the regular season winds down.
"The Dodgers' splash signings of Tucker and Edwin Diaz in last season's free agency were the cause of much handwringing about LA's economic dominance," Doolittle wrote.
"While those high-level, targeted acquisitions looked like no-brainers at the time, the first year of both deals could hardly have gone worse. Together, Tucker and Diaz are at minus-1.0 bWAR for their Dodgers debuts while earning a combined $47 million. Ouch."
How Has Edwin Diaz Been for the Dodgers?
Diaz was the first of the two to sign, inking a three-year, $69 million contract with the Dodgers.
The Dodgers made him the highest-paid closer by average annual salary, and as the season winds down, that contract is looking like an utter disaster. In 16 appearances this year, Diaz has posted a 11.85 ERA, 2.56 WHIP and 19 strikeouts in 13.2 innings.
The 32-year-old has blown four saves out of 11 opportunities. On top of that, batters are hitting a staggering .385 against him in Los Angeles.
Diaz has also struggled with injuries. He's missed significant time due to elbow surgery and is currently on the injured list with neck inflammation.
His lack of results, inconsistencies and injuries have cast serious doubt on whether he will even make the Dodgers' postseason roster.
How Has Kyle Tucker Been for the Dodgers?
As for Tucker, he's been available, but just hasn't performed.
The Dodgers signed the 29-year-old to a lucrative deal, carrying the highest present-day average annual value (AAV) in MLB history at $57.1 million per year.
However, Tucker hasn't performed at that level for most of the season.
The overall numbers alone are worrisome. Tucker is batting .226 with 15 home runs, 66 RBIs, 11 stolen bases and 113 hits in 500 at-bats. His OPS is just .701.
Tucker will continue to get everyday opportunities through the end of the regular season and the posteason. If he can play well in October, all will be forgotten from his disappointing first year.
Sign up for our free newsletter and follow us on X/Twitter and Facebook for the latest news.
Ricardo Sandoval is a freelance writer with On SI. He is a graduate of California State University, Northridge, and specializes in sports writing, particularly in MLB, NBA and NFL. He previously served as an Associate Editor for Dodgers Nation and has worked with Newsweek and The Sporting News.
Follow @_RicardoSand

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Edwin Diaz Dealt Bad News on Future With Los Angeles Dodgers
item.dc:creator: Dibyendu Mondal
item.description: Edwin Diaz signed a three-year, $69 million contract in December. It made him baseball's highest-paid reliever by average annual salary. His first season for the Los Angeles Dodgers has not matched that price tag. Diaz opened the year on a rocky note. He allowed one run through his first five outings. Two rough appearances followed. Doctors then found loose bodies in his right elbow. He had arthroscopic surgery and missed roughly 100 days. He returned in late July and posted mixed results. The D
item.content:encoded:
Edwin Diaz signed a three-year, $69 million contract in December. It made him baseball's highest-paid reliever by average annual salary. His first season for the Los Angeles Dodgers has not matched that price tag.
Diaz opened the year on a rocky note. He allowed one run through his first five outings. Two rough appearances followed.
Doctors then found loose bodies in his right elbow. He had arthroscopic surgery and missed roughly 100 days.
He returned in late July and posted mixed results. The Dodgers placed him back on the injured list Aug. 18. This time, doctors diagnosed inflammation on the right side of his neck.
Diaz has an 11.85 ERA in 16 appearances this season. He has thrown 13 2/3 innings for the Los Angeles Dodgers. The right-hander has struck out 19 batters and walked 10.
That uneven form has created real uncertainty about his spot on the postseason roster.
Edwin Diaz's Roster Spot Now in Doubt
insider Ken Rosenthal addressed Diaz's situation on the show "Foul Territory." He said the Dodgers will pick their 26 best players, regardless of salary.
The club has called this year's pitching staff its deepest ever heading into October.
Rosenthal added that if evaluators view Diaz as not good enough, the Dodgers will leave him off. Rosenthal called it a "win-at-all-costs kind of industry."
Manager Dave Roberts has not guaranteed Diaz a spot either. "We have to go with our best pitchers," Roberts said. Diaz has not pitched well enough yet during his rehab assignment.
He allowed five runs while recording two outs in his Sept. 13 outing. He is set for another rehab appearance Sept. 16, with an expected return in late September.
The stakes are real. The Dodgers clinched a playoff berth Monday with a win over the Cincinnati Reds.
Latest Updates on Edwin Diaz, Shohei Ohtani
The Dodgers updated their injury report this week. Several key players remain sidelined heading into the stretch run.
Diaz remains on the 15-day injured list with neck inflammation. He is on a rehab assignment with Triple-A Oklahoma City.
Shohei Ohtani is on the 15-day injured list with a left knee and right biceps injury, retroactive to Sept. 8. He could return as a hitter as soon as Sept. 23. He is not expected to pitch again until 2027. He began a swing progression Sept. 15, hitting off a tee.
Outfielder Andy Pages has a fractured left hand. He landed on the 10-day injured list Aug. 22. He has progressed to hitting baseballs off a machine, with an expected return in late September as well.

item.title: [Friars on Base] Padres hoping Edwin Díaz makes Dodgers' playoff roster as struggles reach breaking point
item.dc:creator: PJ Potter
item.description: It has been a nightmare season for three-time Reliever of the Year Edwin Díaz. In his first year with the Los Angeles Dodgers, he's made two trips to the injured list, all while logging a -1.3 bWAR and 11.85 ERA. The Dodgers were hoping that Díaz would help cement a third straight World Series title, but considering every bit of struggle from the 32-year-old closer, they may keep him off the postseason roster if no sign of progress is being made. “We have to go with our best pitchers, as far as
item.content:encoded:
It has been a nightmare season for three-time Reliever of the Year Edwin Díaz. In his first year with the Los Angeles Dodgers, he's made two trips to the injured list, all while logging a -1.3 bWAR and 11.85 ERA.
The Dodgers were hoping that Díaz would help cement a third straight World Series title, but considering every bit of struggle from the 32-year-old closer, they may keep him off the postseason roster if no sign of progress is being made.
“We have to go with our best pitchers, as far as performance, talent, all that stuff,” Roberts said in The Athletic's report. “So my bet is that he will be (on the roster). But again, there’s got to be some kind of evidence or something for us, again, to sort of bet on. And so my bet is yes, but we still got to see something.”
The San Diego Padres, among every other National League postseason hopeful, are crossing their fingers that the Dodgers ultimately keep Díaz on the roster.
Padres fans can finally point to a Dodgers' problem with merit
For the last few seasons, it felt like the Dodgers were invincible. Seemingly every MVP and All-Star joined the organization, conjuring up a super team that has baseball fans worried about a potential lockout this upcoming offseason.
So for once, San Diego fans can actually look at Los Angeles and smile as they hold an advantage over them. The Padres have a much better closer, and it's not even close to being an argument anymore.
Mason Miller's 1.12 ERA, 0.855 WHIP, and league-best 37 saves make the Padres that much better of a contending playoff team. The Dodgers can't say about their closer anymore. In a rehab stint this past Sunday with Triple-A Oklahoma City, Díaz was torched for five runs in 0.2 innings against minor leaguers, surrendering three walks and two hits.
Entering Tuesday's games, the Padres would face the Dodgers in the NLDS if they were to advance out of the Wild Card round. The Friars, and their fans, are hoping that Dodgers feel forced to have Díaz on the postseason roster.
After all, he is getting paid $60 million by Los Angeles over the next three seasons. He's not the easiest guy to part with.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers recently sent Edwin Díaz on his second rehab assignment of the season. His first stint in Oklahoma City — back when he was rehabbing following elbow surgery — didn't go well. He posted a 10.80 ERA in just 1⅓ innings. Impossibly, however, he's been even worse his second time around.
Díaz has made four rehab outings for the so far. His first was almost spotless (he gave up a walk), but his second lasted just ⅔ innings after he gave up a run on two walks. The third was a promising bounce back — one hit, one walk, no earned runs in a full inning — but his latest was a downright disaster.
On Sunday, Diaz gave up five earned runs on two hits, a hit by pitch, and three walks. He was yanked before he could get out of the inning.
The Dodgers still have a few days before they need to make a roster move, but under no circumstances can he be used in close games, not even if they clinch a postseason berth. The Atlanta Braves are still within striking distance for a first-round bye, and the Dodgers can't afford to lose it.
When Díaz comes back, the only acceptable situation to use him in would be a blowout, and even then, fans would find it impossible to trust him. Although Tanner Scott appears to be turning back into a pumpkin, even he would lend the team greater reassurances in close games.
Edwin Díaz's latest rehab meltdown should force Dodgers to leave him off their postseason roster
It also puts the Dodgers in an uncomfortable but undeniable position: Díaz can't be on the postseason roster.
Roki Sasaki is likely to go back to the rotation when he returns from injury, but repeating his role as LA's lights-out postseason closer could be on the docket if Scott fails to prove himself trustworthy. Tyler Glasnow is also expected to move to the bullpen in October, so the Dodgers could even audition him in the role.
While the Dodgers are still the heavy favorites to win the World Series, it'll be an undeniable embarrassment to the team if they do it without Díaz — their $69 million man — who they haven't been able to figure out all season long.
